title: Not by shaving the head (263–272)
hookLine: a shaven head doesn't make a monk; the one who quiets evil is the true samana
last: WISDOM CAN LIVE IN ANY BODY.

cards: You can buy the running shoes, the fitness watch and the matching outfit, and post a photo at the start of the trail. None of it runs a single mile.
You can set a meditation cushion in the corner of your bedroom, beautifully lit, with a candle and a small statue. The cushion doesn't sit.
Owning the gear is one thing and doing the work is another, and the gear is always easier. Even in the Buddha's day, people noticed that robes and a shaved head could be worn by anyone.
Chapter nineteen goes on to test the titles of the holy life.

teach.b: Verse two sixty-four, in Max Müller's translation: "Not by tonsure does an undisciplined man who speaks falsehood become a Samana". A samaṇa was a wandering renunciant, one who had left home for the spiritual life.
Then the verse plays with the word. Two sixty-five: "He who always quiets the evil, whether small or large, he is called a Samana (a quiet man), because he has quieted all evil."
In Pali, samaṇa sounds like the verb for calming, quieting.
So the real samaṇa is the one who has quieted harm, not the one with the haircut. The chapter does this again and again. A bhikkhu, a monk, isn't one just because he asks for alms.

teach.h: MONK, SAGE, NOBLE: RETURNED TO MEANING.
teach.b: A muni, a sage, isn't one just because he keeps silent, from mona, silence; a true sage weighs things well: "he who in this world weighs both sides is called a Muni."
An ariya, a noble one, isn't one if he harms living beings; he's called noble "because he has pity on all living creatures". Every title gets turned back to what it's supposed to mean.
Then the chapter warns even the sincere. Vows, learning, deep meditation, solitude: none of it is a reason to relax.
"Bhikshu, be not confident as long as thou hast not attained the extinction of desires." This isn't a dig at monks; monks and nuns themselves chant these verses.
It's a mirror for anyone with a label: Buddhist, meditator, good person.
The practice makes it. The label never does.

how: Monks and nuns shave their heads and wear robes as signs of renunciation, and the tradition itself teaches, in verses like these, that the signs matter only when the practice behind them is real.

games.q: what does “not by shaving the head” mean?
o: only a shaved head proves you have left home
a true monk is made by quieting harm, not looks
shaving the head is forbidden on the path

games.q: match each title to what really makes it.
p: has quieted harm, small or large
has pity on all living beings

s: a shaved head makes someone a samaṇa, says verse 264
"not by tonsure does an undisciplined man who speaks falsehood become a Samana."
the verses redefine each title by what it should mean
samaṇa, bhikkhu, muni and ariya are each turned back to their qualities.
these verses are only criticism aimed at monks from outside
monks and nuns chant them; they're a mirror for anyone with a label.

games.q: you've kept your vows, studied hard and sat long retreats. can you relax now, sure you've arrived?
o: not yet: be not confident until desire is extinguished.
only if a teacher says so.
games.why: "Bhikshu, be not confident as long as thou hast not attained the extinction of desires." the practice keeps going.

practice: For these two minutes there's no audience at all: no photo, no streak, no label, just the breath coming in and going out. If a thought shows up, I'm good at this, or I'm bad at this, notice that it's another label, and let it go.
Quiet one small agitation, then the next; that's all a samaṇa does.

wordCard.voice: Not by shaving the head. Verse two sixty-five: a shaven head doesn't make a samaṇa; the one who has quieted harm, small or large, is one.

orig.note: Pali: a wandering renunciant; verse 265 plays on it as the one who has quieted (samita) harm.

carryVoice: Your line: the practice makes it. Not the tonsure, not the title. That's day two hundred eight.
